title: Interactive Runtime Debug & Experimentation Playbook
author: Priya Khatri
summary: A compact, hands-on playbook for on-call and runtime engineers to perform interactive debugging, reproducible micro-experiments, and short-turn kernel scheduling investigations using production-like traces and the benchmarking harness.
body:
Overview

Purpose: Provide a pragmatic, repeatable workflow for interactive triage and controlled experiments that span kernel scheduling, KV-cache behavior, and request-path latency. This playbook is intended for engineers working on the serving runtime who need to go from a symptom (tail latency, noisy interference, or regression) to an actionable hypothesis and safe mitigation within a single on-call shift.

Scope: Low-latency, GPU-backed inference services only (hosted and dedicated modes). This playbook assumes access to the runtime sandbox environment, the benchmark harness, and trace replay tools. It is NOT a full incident RCA; use the incident process doc for long-running investigations.

When to use this playbook
- New or rising P95/P99 latency after a deploy or kernel rollout.
- Regressions observed in profiling signals that are reproducible on a small set of requests (microbursts).
- Scheduling anomalies: unexplained preemption, unfair kernel allocation, or unexpected slot consumption.
- Before proposing a scheduler change or kernel rollout; use this to validate locally first.

Prerequisites and access
- Credentials: sandbox-cluster role + read access to telemetry.
- Tools: redwood-trace-replay, redwood-bench, rtm-prof, kernel-qa harness.
- Data: a minimal shadow trace that reproduces the symptom (<= 200 requests ideal).
- Owners: runtime on-call and the kernel-scheduler rotation engineer must be paged for any experiment that touches production kernel parameters.

Quick checklist (one-line)
1) Freeze in-flight deploys and confirm hypothesis owner.
2) Capture a 2–10 minute shadow trace with full kernel and scheduling annotations.
3) Reproduce locally in the sandbox with trace-replay + profiler.
4) Run controlled microbenchmarks to isolate kernel scheduling or KV-cache effects.
5) Apply temporary mitigation (priority tweak, admission limit) and monitor for 30–60 minutes.
6) If mitigation holds, draft a follow-up experiment plan for rollout.

Interactive Triage Workflow (detailed)
1. Capture and annotate evidence
   - Capture a lightweight trace from the affected node(s) using: redwood-collect-trace --duration 120 --include-kernel --include-kvcache --tags p99-investigation --out /tmp/trace.pb
   - Attach the trace to the ticket and add the on-call rotation engineer as reviewer.

2. Build a minimal repro corpus
   - Select a 20–200 request sample focusing on the symptom window. Prefer short prompts if kernel scheduling is suspected, longer prompts if KV-cache warmup is implicated.
   - Sanitize any customer PII before replay.

3. Replay in sandbox with tracing enabled
   - Command: redwood-trace-replay --trace /tmp/trace.pb --sandbox cluster:staging-sandbox --profile rtm-prof --output ./replay-results
   - Expected deliverables: wall-clock timeline, per-kernel latency breakdown, scheduler decision log.

4. Hypothesis formation and quick A/B
   - Form 1–2 hypotheses (e.g., "priority inversion due to background batcher", "KV-cache cold-start caused extra kernel ops").
   - Run A/B by toggling one variable at a time: scheduler policy string, kernel hint flag, or batcher concurrency setting. Use redwood-bench --micro to run 3x 30-second samples per variant.

5. Controlled microbench recipes
   - Kernel scheduling isolation test
     1) Baseline: rep-play with default scheduler.
     2) Variant A: switch to policy="strict-preempt" on sandbox nodes.
     3) Variant B: set kernel_credit_limit=0.8.
     4) Compare P50/P95/P99 and per-kernel tail latency.
   - KV-cache warmup test
     1) Baseline: cold KV cache.
     2) Variant: preload cache with prefix replay.
     3) Coverage: measure kernel invocation count per request.

6. Telemetry to collect and look at
   - Required signals (minimum): request.timeline.ms, kernel.exec.ms (per kernel id), scheduler.decision.reason, kernel.cpu_ns, gpu_active_ms, kvcache.hit_rate, admission.queue_depth.
   - Secondary signals: container.swap, gpu_thermal_cstate, preemption.count.

Investigation decision matrix
| Symptom | Likely root area | First experiment | Mitigation to try | Rollout decision 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Spiky P99 with many small requests | Scheduler priority inversion | Strict-preempt policy A/B | Temporarily raise SLO priority for affected route | If repeatable, schedule scheduler policy rollout with canary 10% |
| Long first-token latency | KV-cache cold start | Preload prefix / forced warmup | Reduce cold-start penalty with small cache-reserve | Require benchmark validation |
| Consistent 10–20% GPU idle | Kernel batching inefficiency | Run microbatcher trace with altered slice size | Adjust batch-slice target and re-evaluate | Gradual rollout |

Experiment safety and guardrails
- Always run experiments in the sandbox and optionally in a single dedicated capacity pool before touching shared production.
- No changes to scheduler kernel code are allowed from the on-call unless signed off by the scheduler owner.
- If experiment alters admission or priority, set conservative timeboxed windows (15–60 minutes) and automated rollback via the console.
- Notify SRE and Customer Success if mitigation affects latency or throughput for paying customers.

Benchmarks and result capture
- Use redwood-bench with the following standard flags for all micro-experiments: --samples 3 --sample-duration 30s --trace-depth kernel,scheduler,kvcache --artifact-dir ./bench-results/<variant>
- Record the following artifacts into the experiment ticket: bench-summary.txt, raw-trace.pb, rtm-prof report, and a short changelog of parameters.

Example commands and snippets
- Capture: redwood-collect-trace --duration 120 --include-kernel --out p99-20260712.trace
- Replay: redwood-trace-replay --trace p99-20260712.trace --sandbox staging-sandbox --profile rtm-prof --out ./replay-output
- Microbench: redwood-bench --micro --route /v1/generate --samples 3 --sample-duration 30 --variant-label kvcache-warmup

Observability and dashboards
- Dashboards to check: "Runtime Kernel Heatmap", "Scheduler Decision Trace", "KV Cache Warmth". Dashboards must show experiment variants side-by-side for easy comparison.
- Annotation: add experiment label in telemetry (experiment_id) so that traces and metrics are queryable (e.g., experiment_id=orch-2026-07-12).

When to escalate to kernel team or SRE
- If A/B variants show >=30% increase in tail kernel latency or a new class of kernel errors (GPU hang, watchdog resets).
- If isolation tests show the behavior reproduces on different hardware families.
- If mitigation requires changes to kernel binaries or driver-level config.

Post-experiment steps and documentation
1) Collate artifacts and fill the experiment summary template (attach to ticket).
2) If mitigation is successful and low-risk, create a rollout PR with canary matrix and perf gates.
3) If unresolved, escalate to a dedicated investigation and consider a small-scale perf-capture party (day-long).

Ownership and contacts
- Runtime on-call: runtime-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Kernel scheduling primary: Marcus Liu (marcus@redwood.example.com)
- Observability / telemetry: Jordan Reyes (jordan@redwood.example.com)

Appendix: minimal telemetry table (paste into dashboards)
| key | description | recommended resolution | alert threshold |
| request.timeline.ms | end-to-end request duration | 1s (aggregate), 100ms (p50/p95) | p99 > 800ms |
| kernel.exec.ms | per-kernel execution latency | 10ms | kernel tail > 250ms |
| scheduler.decision.reason | text tag for decision path | event | new decision type seen |
| kvcache.hit_rate | rolling 1m hit rate | 10s | drop > 15% relative to baseline |

Appendix B: safe experiment checklist (must be completed before any infra change)
- [ ] Sandbox replay reproduces symptom.
- [ ] Experiment owner assigned and pager notified.
- [ ] Rollback plan documented.
- [ ] Telemetry annotation ready.
- [ ] Bench artifacts target location specified.

Notes and rationale
- This playbook prioritizes fast, low-risk verification loops. The goal is to produce reproducible artifacts (traces and microbench results) that enable deterministic reasoning about scheduler and kernel interactions. By keeping experiments short and well-annotated we decrease blast radius and accelerate safe rollouts.

Related reading
- See the runtime telemetry data model page for field definitions.
- See the kernel QA harness README for instructions on building kernel variants.
